title: How Can God Be Sovereign and Humans Still Be Free?
subtitle: Compatibilism, libertarian freedom, and Molinism. Three accounts of how God's rule and the human will can both be real.
triageNote: That God is sovereign and that human beings are genuinely responsible are both taught plainly in Scripture. The whole church confesses both. What divides faithful believers is how the two fit, what human freedom actually is, and whether it must include the power to have done otherwise. Philosophers and theologians have argued that for centuries. It has never been a test of orthodoxy. It runs between people who pray to the same Lord and answer to Him for the same choices. Hold the two truths, God's rule and your responsibility, with both hands. Hold your theory of how they cohere with humility. Here Scripture asserts the pair more clearly than it explains the joinery.
question: Scripture never once apologizes for holding two things together that human logic strains to hold. God works all things according to His will. And you are fully responsible for what you do. It commands you to choose, warns you, pleads with you, and judges you, treating your choices as really yours. It also says God turns the king's heart, grants repentance, opens the heart to believe, and works in you to will and to act. So what is human freedom. Is it the power, at the moment of choosing, to have done otherwise, an open future genuinely up to you. Or is it acting according to your own strongest desire, uncoerced, even though God ordains what that desire will be. Or is there a third thing, a freedom God knows so exhaustively that He can sovereignly weave it into His plan without overriding it. The answer you give decides what you think happens in the deepest moment of human life. That is the moment a person turns to God or away from Him.
whyItMatters:
This is not a puzzle for people with time on their hands. It is the question underneath your guilt and underneath your hope. When you sin, is it truly your fault, or were you only doing what was determined for you. When you repent, did you do it, or did God do it in you. And does the answer change whether the repentance is real. When you plead with a wandering son to come home, are you appealing to a will that can genuinely turn, or performing a script already written. Every serious moment of the moral and spiritual life presses this question. You are already answering it by how you live, whether or not you have ever named your answer.

It also decides how you read the gospel offer. When Christ says come to me, all who are weary, is that an offer a person can accept by a power of contrary choice, or a call that creates the very response it commands in those God has chosen. Whole accounts of conversion, assurance, and evangelism hang on which freedom is real. Get it wrong toward determinism and you can drift into fatalism. Why pray, why strive, it is all settled. Get it wrong toward autonomy and you can drift into a God who is finally waiting on you, hoping you will choose Him, His purposes hostage to your will. The historic accounts are all trying to keep both feet planted, on God's real sovereignty and your real responsibility. The question is which account keeps its balance.

And it shapes how you bear the unbearable. The person who believes their choices could always have gone otherwise carries their failures one way. The person who believes God ordained even their worst hour carries them another. Neither carries them carelessly. You are not choosing a theory of the will. You are choosing how to understand the most consequential thing you ever do, which is to turn, or refuse to turn, toward your Maker.

positions.name: Compatibilism
positions.inOneLine: Freedom is acting according to your own strongest desire without external coercion. That is fully compatible with God ordaining what you will desire and do. So you are genuinely free and genuinely responsible.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin by defining freedom the way I actually use the word. Most of the disagreement is a disagreement about definitions hiding as a disagreement about the Bible. To be free, I say, is to do what you most want to do, without anyone forcing your hand. When you chose what to eat this morning, no one held a gun to your head. You acted from your own desire, and that is freedom, real freedom, the only kind you have ever actually experienced. Notice what this freedom does not require. It does not require that your desire came from nowhere, uncaused. Your desires have causes, your nature, your history, your loves. And yet your choices are no less yours for being the choices your nature produces. This is why I am called a compatibilist. I hold that this freedom is fully compatible with God ordaining, from before the foundation of the world, what you would desire and do.

Why do I read the Bible this way. Because the Bible itself does, constantly. It holds people fully responsible for acts it also says God ordained, and it never treats the two as a contradiction needing resolution. Joseph's brothers freely, guiltily meant evil, and God meant the same act for good. The men who crucified Jesus did it by their own wicked will, and they did it by the definite plan of God. Most strikingly, God hardens Pharaoh's heart and Pharaoh hardens his own heart, both said of the same events, and Pharaoh is fully culpable. The biblical writers see no problem here. The freedom they assume is the freedom to act from your own heart, and the God they know ordains the heart and its acts without forcing them. Proverbs says the heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps. Both clauses are true at once. Compatibilism is simply the refusal to delete either one.

Here is the deep thing this view protects, the thing I am most jealous for. It is the sovereignty of grace in salvation. If freedom required the power of contrary choice, then in the moment of conversion the final, decisive factor would be me, my exercise of that power, and grace would be a help I complete rather than a gift that saves. But Scripture says God grants repentance, opens the heart, gives the new birth that no one chooses any more than a corpse chooses to rise. Lazarus did not contribute his cooperation to his resurrection. He came out because the word that called him also raised him. So in conversion God does not violate my will, He changes it, He gives me a new heart with new desires, and then I freely, gladly, come, doing exactly what I now most want to do. That is not coercion. That is the most liberating thing that has ever happened to me, and only a compatibilist account can call it both free and entirely of grace.

What do I struggle with, and I will not dodge it. My sharpest critics say that if God ordains my desires, and I act from those desires, then God is the ultimate author of my sin, and my responsibility is a fiction with a friendly face. I feel the force of that. I answer that God ordains that I sin without being the one who sins. The sinful desire is truly mine, arising from my own corrupt heart. And the guilt attaches to the desire and the deed, both of which are mine, not to the decree, which is righteous and aims at good. I hold that distinction firmly. But I confess I cannot fully illuminate how an ordained act is yet wholly mine and not at all God's. At the bottom of my view there is a mystery I confess rather than dissolve, the same mystery I find the biblical writers content to leave standing.
advocates: D. A. Carson (Divine Sovereignty and Human Responsibility)

positions.name: Libertarian freedom
positions.inOneLine: A choice is free only if, at the moment of choosing, the person genuinely could have chosen otherwise. This power of contrary choice is what makes us responsible and makes love real.
positions.bestCase:
Let me ask you to consult something you cannot doubt, the inside of your own moral experience. When you face a real choice, a temptation you could yield to or resist, you know, with a certainty deeper than any argument, that it is genuinely up to you which way you go. After you do wrong, you do not merely feel regret. You feel that you could have done otherwise, that the door was open and you chose the worse one, and that knowledge is the root of your guilt. Remove that, tell me the door was never really open, that I was always going to choose exactly what I chose, and you have not described my freedom. You have described a sophisticated puppet that feels strings it cannot see. The freedom I claim, libertarian freedom, is just this. In the moment of a real choice, more than one outcome was truly within my power. The could have done otherwise is not a luxury added to freedom. It is freedom.

Why do I find this in Scripture. Because the entire moral structure of the Bible assumes it. God sets before Israel life and death, blessing and curse, and says choose life, and the command is not a cruelty addressed to people who cannot obey it. The prophets plead, turn, why will you die, and the plea is real because the turning is genuinely possible. Joshua says choose this day whom you will serve. Jesus laments that He would have gathered Jerusalem and they were not willing, and that lament makes no sense if their unwillingness was the only thing they could ever have been. I cannot make the thousand pleadings and warnings and offers of Scripture honest if the people addressed never had it in their power to respond. God does not mock. When He says choose, He means a real fork in the road.

And here is the deepest thing my view protects, deeper than responsibility. It protects love. Love that is determined is not love. If God ordained that I love Him, scripted my devotion from before the world began so that I could never have withheld it, then my love is His own act ventriloquized through me. He is finally loving Himself through a mechanism He built. But Scripture says God seeks worshipers, grieves rejection, rejoices over the one who comes home. That only makes sense if the heart that turns to Him could have stayed away. God wanted lovers, not mirrors. So He made us able to refuse Him, which is the terrible dignity He gave His image-bearers and the reason hell is a monument to a freedom God honored even when it broke His heart.

Let me name where I am pressed hardest, because I owe it. The strongest blow against me is the sovereignty of God in salvation, those texts that say God grants repentance, opens hearts, gives the new birth, and that no one comes unless the Father draws him. If salvation is finally up to my power of contrary choice, am I not making myself, at the last and decisive point, my own savior, the one who supplies what grace could not. I answer that grace genuinely enables the choice, that God's drawing is real and even prevenient, going before me and freeing my bound will. But this freed will must still actually turn, and the turning is mine. I grant that this is the seam my critics press hardest, the worry that I have left the decisive vote with the creature. I hold my answer knowing the weight of the objection. I cannot surrender the conviction that when God says choose, the choice is real, without losing the God who pleads.

positions.name: Molinism and middle knowledge
positions.inOneLine: Human freedom is libertarian, the real power of contrary choice. And God remains fully sovereign, because He knows what every free creature would freely do in every circumstance. He arranges the world accordingly.
positions.bestCase:
I want to offer you both of the things the first two views make you choose between. And I want to show you that you do not have to choose. From the libertarian I take the whole truth that real freedom means the power of contrary choice. When God pleads choose life He addresses a will that can actually turn either way. And love which could not have been withheld is not love. I will not give that up. But from the compatibilist I take, just as firmly, that God is meticulously sovereign, that all things really do serve the counsel of His will, that nothing in history is a surprise or a setback to Him. The first two views think these commitments collide. I hold that they do not. The key that opens the door is an idea as old as the sixteenth century, middle knowledge.

Here is the idea, and watch how much it carries. God knows three kinds of things. He knows all necessary truths, what must be. He knows, by His free decision, what He wills to do. And in between, He knows what every possible free creature would freely do in every possible circumstance, the true counterfactuals of freedom. He knows that if this person were placed in these exact conditions, she would freely choose this, not because He forces it, but because that is what she, in her freedom, would do. Now see what God can do with that knowledge. Before creating, He surveys every possible world and every free creature's free response within it. Then God sovereignly selects which world to bring about, choosing the arrangement in which free creatures, doing only and exactly what they freely would do, accomplish His purposes. The result is staggering. Providence is total and meticulous, every detail serving God's plan. And freedom is fully libertarian, every choice genuinely the creature's own with the power to have done otherwise. Nothing is forced, and nothing is left to chance.

Let me show you the texts that I think only my view reads without strain. God tells David that if he stays in Keilah, Saul will come and the men of Keilah will surrender him. David leaves, and neither thing ever happens, yet God knew truly what those free men would have done. Jesus says that if the mighty works done in Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented in sackcloth, a free choice in a circumstance that never occurred. These are counterfactuals of creaturely freedom, stated as known facts by an omniscient God. They are exactly what middle knowledge says God knows. And at the cross, Acts says Jesus was delivered by the definite plan of God and crucified by lawless men, both true with no tension on my account. God placed the actors knowing what they would freely do, so the plan was wholly His and the sin wholly theirs.

Where am I pressed hardest, and I will be honest, because the objection is genuinely formidable. It is called the grounding objection. Before I exist, what makes it true that I, in those circumstances, would freely deny Christ rather than confess Him. The choice is supposed to be free, so it cannot be made true by God's decree, or I lose the libertarian freedom my whole system is built to keep. But if nothing grounds it, my critics ask whether there is any fact there at all for God to know, whether middle knowledge has an object. I answer that these are simply truths about what free persons would do, true in themselves. An omniscient God knows all truths, including these. And free choices by their nature are not made true by anything prior to them, which is what freedom means. I think that answer holds. But I will not pretend the knife-edge is comfortable. I balance my whole account on it, and a sharp critic from either side will go straight for it. I respect them for it. I am trying to keep two treasures at once, and that is harder than keeping only one.
advocates: William Lane Craig (The Only Wise God)

biblicalEvidence.summary: Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant the same act for good. Jesus was delivered by the definite plan of God and crucified by the hands of lawless men. The same acts are at once freely, guiltily human and definitely ordained by God, with no hint that the two cancel.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for libertarian freedom, since the acts are both fully culpable and definitely planned. Compatibilism holds that together more easily than a view requiring the power to have done otherwise.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Libertarian freedom reads delivered up and meant for good as God purposing and overruling freely chosen evil He did not author, the men retaining the real power to have refused. Molinism reads them as God arranging, through middle knowledge, circumstances in which He knew the agents would freely do what they did, so the plan is God's and the free, guilty act is theirs without remainder.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to act for His good pleasure. Human working and divine working are set side by side in the same sentence. God works the very willing that you then do.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against libertarian freedom. God is said to work in you to will, producing the will that acts, rather than merely enabling a choice left finally to you.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Libertarian freedom reads God works in you to will as God's enabling and empowering grace that makes the willing possible while leaving the actual willing yours, the for therefore grounding human effort in divine help, not erasing it. Molinism reads it as God sovereignly bringing about, through His chosen arrangement of circumstances and grace, the free willing He foreknew, both clauses true at once.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps. The lot is cast in the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord. Real human planning and real divine determination of the outcome are affirmed together as a settled truth.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against any view that makes the human choice the final, undetermined factor. The Lord establishes the steps and decides the lot.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Libertarian freedom reads these as God's sovereign freedom to direct and overrule outcomes when His purposes require, alongside genuine human deliberation, and notes proverbs state general truths, not a metaphysics of every act. Molinism reads them as God establishing the steps precisely through His knowledge of how the man would freely plan, sovereignty exercised through free agency rather than against it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse, therefore choose life. Choose this day whom you will serve. God places a genuine choice before the people and commands them to make it, treating the decision as really within their power.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against compatibilism. The command to choose seems to assume the people genuinely could go either way, not merely that they would act from a heart already determined.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Compatibilism reads choose life as a real and serious command addressed to real wills, fulfilled by those whose hearts God renews, the command revealing duty and exposing inability rather than proving the power of contrary choice. The call is no less genuine for that. Molinism reads it as God genuinely setting a libertarian choice before them, the very kind of free decision His middle knowledge encompasses, so the command and divine sovereignty stand together.

biblicalEvidence.summary: How often would I have gathered your children, and you were not willing. As I live, declares the Lord, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that he turn and live. God's longing to gather and His call to turn meet a human unwillingness. Scripture presents it as genuinely resistible.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for compatibilism, which must explain how God genuinely longs to gather those whose unwillingness He has, on its account, ordained.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Compatibilism reads these as God's real revealed will, His genuine command and delight in repentance, distinct from His secret decree, so the longing is sincere and the unwillingness is the people's own culpable hardness, both true. Molinism reads them as God's sincere desire for all to turn, with the unwillingness a free refusal God foreknew, honored even as He grieves it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God tells David what Saul and the men of Keilah would do, though the events never occur. Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen the miracles Chorazin saw. God knows truly what free agents would have freely done in circumstances that never came to pass.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against any account with no place for counterfactuals of freedom. These are precisely such counterfactuals, affirmed by Scripture.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Compatibilism reads them as God's knowledge of what would result from His own possible arrangements, or as expressions heightening human responsibility, not a distinct faculty of middle knowledge prior to His decree. Libertarian freedom reads them as God's exhaustive foreknowledge including the conditional, without committing to the full Molinist apparatus of pre-volitional world selection. Molinism reads them as direct evidence of the middle knowledge its whole account requires.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God is faithful, and He will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation He will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. God so arranges circumstances that a real way out is always available to the tempted believer.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Pressed against a determinism in which the outcome of temptation is simply fixed. A genuine way of escape is promised as available to be taken.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Compatibilism reads the way of escape as genuinely provided and genuinely taken by those whose renewed hearts God moves to take it, the promise sure precisely because God works the endurance He requires. Molinism reads it as God, by middle knowledge, arranging circumstances so that an escape the believer could freely take is always present, His faithfulness guaranteeing the option without forcing the choice. Libertarian freedom reads it as proof that the believer always retains a real, takeable alternative to sinning.

weighing:
My judgment, given as one pastor thinking in front of you and not as a verdict you must share to be my brother. I hold it the more carefully because this question reaches all the way down into how a person understands their own guilt and their own hope.

I lean toward compatibilism, and let me tell you the honest reason. It is not a philosophical preference but a cluster of texts I cannot make quiet. Philippians says God works in me to will, the willing itself and not just the room to will. The new birth is described as a thing done to me, like a resurrection, not a thing I contribute to. Lazarus did not vote on coming out of the tomb. When I am most honest about my own conversion, I do not experience it as the moment my power of contrary choice tipped the scale. I experience it as the moment I was found, given a new heart that wanted what it had never wanted, after which I came freely because I finally, gladly, wanted to. Compatibilism is the only account that lets me call that both entirely of grace and truly my own free coming. I am not willing to surrender either half.

But the libertarian presses me exactly where I am thinnest, and I feel it. Consider the thousand pleadings of Scripture, choose life, turn, why will you die, and above all the tears of Christ over a Jerusalem that would not. These are hard to read as fully sincere if the unwillingness was the only thing those people could ever have done. I lean on the distinction between God's revealed will, which genuinely commands and longs, and His secret will, which ordains. I believe that distinction is real and biblical, but I hold it as a place where I trust more than I see. And the Molinist has built the most elegant machine anyone has offered for keeping both treasures. On my better days I think middle knowledge may simply be right, a way to grant the libertarian his real power of contrary choice while keeping God meticulously sovereign. On my harder days the grounding objection genuinely troubles me, and I cannot make it vanish.

So I land here, loosely. I believe God truly ordains all that comes to pass and that my choices are truly mine and truly culpable. And I confess that the deepest account of how the freed will and the sovereign decree meet runs down past where my sight reaches. I would rather hold both biblical truths in tension than purchase a tidy theory by quietly dropping one of them. And I have learned, over years, that the believer who lands on libertarian freedom and the believer who lands on Molinism are not less in awe of God's grace than I am. They are guarding a corner of the truth I am tempted to leave unwatched.
charitableDisagreement:
It is easy to weaponize this debate. The compatibilist can sneer that the libertarian worships human autonomy and has smuggled the creature onto the throne. The libertarian can sneer that the compatibilist worships a puppeteer and has made God the author of sin and hell a cruelty. Both sneers are caricatures. Both have done real damage, sending people away from a church that seemed to make them choose between God's power and God's love. Refuse the sneer.

Hear what each is actually guarding. The compatibilist is guarding the sheer sovereignty of grace, the truth that salvation is God's work from first to last and that a dead man does not assist his own resurrection. He is guarding the refusal to leave any corner of reality, including the human will, outside God's rule. The libertarian is guarding the sincerity of God's pleadings and the reality of love. When God says choose He means it, and a love that could not have been withheld is no love at all. The Molinist is guarding the hope that you never had to choose between those two, that a wise enough God holds both His meticulous sovereignty and our real freedom without sacrificing either. None of these is the position of a person who loves God less. Each is a watchman on a wall the others have turned their back to.

So is this a hill to die on. The two truths, that God is sovereign and that you are responsible, are near the heart of the faith. A believer who lets go of either has lost something he will need when he stands before God and when he kneels in the dark. But the theory of how they cohere, the in-house argument among compatibilism and libertarian freedom and Molinism, is a second-order question. The church has carried it unresolved for centuries, in the same congregations, at the same Table, among people who would each die for the Lord they answer to. Hold the sovereignty and the responsibility with both hands. Hold your account of their joinery with a lighter one. Be slow to doubt the faith of the believer who diagrams the seam differently than you do. When the prodigal is on the road home, the compatibilist says grace drew him and the libertarian says he turned and the Molinist says both. All three run to meet him, which is the only thing the father in the story actually does.

relatedDebates.topic: Providence and the government of all things
relatedDebates.note: The freedom question and the providence question are one coin seen from two sides. What human freedom is decides how God can govern it. The providence page in this set takes up the wider doctrine of God's rule, where these same accounts are applied to evil, suffering, and the running of the whole world.

relatedDebates.topic: Election and the order of salvation
relatedDebates.note: How a person comes to faith, whether grace is irresistible, whether the will cooperates, whether God elects on the basis of foreseen faith, is the soteriology page's territory. It is the place this debate becomes most pastorally sharp. It asks who finally decides a soul's turning to God.

relatedDebates.topic: The problem of evil and the free-will defense
relatedDebates.note: Libertarian freedom underwrites the most influential answer to the problem of evil, the free-will defense. It argues that a world with genuinely free creatures capable of love is worth the risk of their freely chosen evil. Whether that defense requires libertarian freedom, or whether a compatibilist theodicy can do the same work, is its own running argument.

relatedDebates.topic: Foreknowledge, time, and the openness debate
relatedDebates.note: At the far edge of this discussion sits open theism. It holds that the future free choices of creatures are not yet there to be known, and so even God does not foreknow them. All three views on this page reject that move and affirm God's exhaustive foreknowledge. But they answer the openness challenge in different ways, which is its own distinct conversation.
